concepts.def: Socialist playwright who wrote the play in 1945.
Brumley, 1912; written looking back from post-war 1945.
Working-class woman whose suicide drives the plot.
Arthur Birling's worldview of profit before people.
Priestley's belief in shared responsibility for all.

walkthroughs.body_html: Priestley wrote the play in 1945 but set it in 1912. The audience in 1945 had lived through two World Wars, the General Strike and the Depression - they knew that Arthur Birling's confident speeches about progress and unsinkable ships would prove disastrously wrong.

Arthur Birling is a self-made factory owner; his wife Sybil is a snobbish charity chairwoman; Sheila and Eric are their adult children; Gerald Croft, Sheila's fiance, links them to old aristocratic money. Each will be revealed as complicit in Eva Smith's death.

Inspector Goole interrupts the celebration with news of a young woman's suicide. As he questions each character in turn, Priestley uses him to deliver a socialist moral: 'We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.'
